extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of physics and philosophy of science (readers interested in foundations of mechanics)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and formulating laws and concepts in classical mechanics with attention to conceptual clarity, empirical scope, and the limits of idealisation (particles, ether, atoms, molecules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit laws to their validated range
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dogmatically assert that laws stated for particles (e.g., Newtonian laws) hold throughout the whole conceptual model (from ether-elements to particles); extend laws only cautiously beyond the range where they have been found to describe experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that laws which suffice for particles of gross 'matter' may not apply to ether-elements, prime-atoms, atoms, or molecules. One must ask whether hypotheses (such as the parallelogram of forces) still suffice when extended to different corpuscles and continually reserve judgment and re-test by experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical obscurity in definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of force, matter, and mass should be interpreted and stated in operational/conceptual terms rather than as metaphysical entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises current textbook definitions as involving metaphysical obscurity and advocates interpreting terms in the writer's own operational sense (e.g., force as a measure related to mass×acceleration). Projection of conceptual machinery into perceived reality should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify reference/frame and relata in laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical laws must indicate relative terms explicitly (e.g., what motion is relative to, to what 'force' is related) to avoid meaningless statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's First Law is criticised for failing to indicate with respect to what a path is a straight line; motion and force are relative and require introduction of a second body or a definite 'frame' for meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about the entity the law addresses (particle vs body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer precise terms ('particle') rather than ambiguous ones ('body') when formulating fundamental laws, because bodies have complex internal motion that obscures the law's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that replacing 'body' by 'particle' removes obscurity, since the motion of composite bodies (spinning, changing axes) is more complex than a simple statement suggests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat force operationally as measure (m×a) not mysterious cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret 'force' as a measurable quantity (product of mass and acceleration) rather than as an imperceptible cause acting 'in a straight line.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second Law's metaphysical language is criticised; the practical interpretation is that force is a measure for some change in motion. Clarify what is changing and in what direction rather than invoking mysterious causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and make explicit idealisations and limits of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that concepts like homogeneity, equal volumes, and 'volume at a point' are conceptual/limit notions not exactly realizable in perception; laws relying on these ideals should state their idealised status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Density, homogeneity, and infinitesimal volumes are admitted to be conceptual limits; the reader must be careful to note these as ideal notions used to construct models that describe perceptual experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define density conceptually via infinitesimal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Density should be defined as the ratio of masses of infinitesimally small equal volumes (or particle masses in the limit) relative to a standard substance, recognising variation point-to-point in heterogeneous bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prefers 'density' (over 'specific gravity') and explains how density classifies substances kinetically and provides the kinetic scale relating geometrical volume to mass in the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume masses of different corpuscle-types are comparable by the same standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious that the mass of an ether-element, prime-atom, atom, molecule, or particle may be of different character and not measurable by the same standard; avoid assuming universally comparable mass ratios across types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text points out that if prime-atoms consist of moving ether, their mass may vanish with motion while constituent ether-elements retain mass; hence one cannot necessarily conceive masses measurable by the same standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider influence of aspect (orientation) on mutual accelerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with non-pointlike corpuscles (atoms, molecules, aggregates) account for how the aspect or orientation they present to each other may affect the absolute magnitudes of their mutual accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes aspect likely plays little role for distant particles but is significant for molecules and structures (crystallisation, magnetisation). The exact influence remains an empirical question to be settled cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for and allow modified action (breakdown of superposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When synthesising motion of complex systems, explicitly test whether component accelerations/forces are altered by the presence of other bodies (modified action) rather than assuming simple vector superposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If B and C together modify each other's influence on A (b→b', c→c'), then synthesis becomes configuration-dependent and the parallelogram of forces does not represent a true combination of forces. Examples include cohesion, chemical interactions, and elastic ether models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve use of the parallelogram of forces to contexts where superposition holds
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the parallelogram (vector addition of forces) only when component forces are unaffected by other bodies; otherwise, it is not a true synthesis of forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parallelogram follows directly when B and C do not modify each other's action. In cases of modified action (e.g., certain atomic/elastic models), component forces depend on the whole configuration and cannot be combined by a fixed parallelogram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek theories that describe widest phenomena with fewest assumptions (parsimony with scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor conceptions/mechanisms that describe the greatest range of phenomena most simply, but do not conflate conceptual convenience with ontological reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The object of science is stated as describing in the fewest words the widest range of phenomena. However, the author warns against projecting conceptual machinery into the phenomenal world (reification) and urges balancing simplicity with empirical adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiment to delimit concepts and imagination to form hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine careful experiments to narrow perceptual facts with the 'brilliant use of scientific imagination' to form broader conceptions that can explain and predict phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that experimental definition of perceptual facts is needed alongside imaginative theoretical work—both are necessary for progress and for forming grand conceptions comparable to Newton or Darwin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about what is meant by inertia and absence of force
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify what 'absence of force' means in context (e.g., absence of surrounding particles leading to no acceleration) rather than treating inertia or force as vague notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting Newton's First Law in terms of surrounding circumstances determining acceleration clarifies inertia: without other particles there is no acceleration. Such restatement avoids platitudes and metaphysical ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse composite-body motion via particle-level principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with composite bodies, base reasoning on particle-level laws (e.g., equality of action and reaction for particles) to justify concepts like center of mass and simplified body-level statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that body-level laws hide internal complexities; the 'center of mass' behaving simply arises from applying particle-level action-reaction principles to the particles constituting the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge multiconstant/material-dependent properties when modelling elasticity and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow for complex, material-dependent (multiconstant) elastic behaviours and interactions which may imply modified action and require more than simple universal laws to describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Kelvin's emphasis on multiconstant elasticity is cited; certain elastic or ether-structure models make modified action essentially true, so one must model such materials with their specific constants rather than universal simplifications.
